problem: Earlier deep-RL visual navigation methods either ran in simple game-like simulators (DeepMind Lab, used by UNREAL and Nav A3C) or relied on frozen ResNet features in small single-room AI2-THOR grid worlds (Zhu et al. 2017 target-driven navigation). Training end-to-end from raw pixels in realistic indoor scenes with sparse rewards was slow and unstable.
motivation: Image-goal navigation from raw camera input is a partially observable problem with high-dimensional observations and a sparse success reward. The bottom convolutional layers are hard to train from noisy RL losses. The authors observe that realistic simulators render depth and semantic segmentation for free, so these can serve as dense supervised signals that shape the shared features. The same signals also allow cheap supervised pre-training on precomputed image datasets.
key_idea: Extend batched A2C and the UNREAL auxiliary tasks with three navigation-specific auxiliary decoders: depth, observation segmentation and target-image segmentation. Combine this with supervised pre-training, a start-distance curriculum and an LSTM memory, to learn image-goal navigation from raw RGB in continuous indoor environments.
insight: Dense auxiliary reconstruction targets give the shallow shared conv layers a useful training signal that the sparse RL loss cannot provide. Predicting the target image's segmentation forces the network to actually use the goal input early in training. On 16 SUNCG houses, adding these tasks cut the frames needed to reach an average episode length of 200 from ≈8·10^6 to ≈3·10^6. This comparison, however, also mixes in supervised pre-training and curriculum, and there is no per-task ablation. A separate DeepMind Lab SeekAvoid experiment shows an LSTM memory clearly beats stacking the past four frames for handling partial observability.
method: Two-stream conv base: observation and target RGB images pass through two weight-shared strided conv layers (no max-pooling). Their outputs are concatenated, then go through two more conv layers and an FC layer.

LSTM core: conv features plus a one-hot previous action and the previous reward clipped to [-1,1] feed an LSTM. The actor (softmax over an affine map), the critic (affine map) and the pixel-control head all read from it.

Batched A2C with off-policy critic: 16 parallel environments, 20-step rollouts with mixed-length bootstrapped n-step returns, and an entropy bonus. Extra critic updates are sampled from a 2,000-step replay buffer. Optimizer is RMSprop with grad-norm clip 0.5 and a linearly decaying LR of 7e-4.

UNREAL auxiliary tasks: reward prediction (3-way classification of the next reward from 3 past frames, sampled with balanced zero/non-zero rewards). Pixel control uses a deconvolutional dueling Q-head trained with n-step Q-learning on absolute pixel-change pseudo-rewards.

Visual-navigation auxiliary tasks: deconvolutional heads on the last conv layer predict downsampled depth, observation segmentation and target segmentation, each trained with MSE at weight 0.1. Segmentation classes are mapped to maximally separated HSB colors. These heads allow supervised pre-training of the conv base (Adam, 30 epochs).

Environment-complexity curriculum: start states are sampled within d_max(τ) = τ·(max state distance) of a target. τ increases linearly from 0.3 to 1.0 during training (from 5M to 10M steps in the SUNCG experiment).
Continuous, noisy AI2-THOR: the simulator was modified for arbitrary-distance moves and rotations with collision physics. Gaussian actuation noise is added (σ = 0.02 m on position, 2° on heading).

setting.backbone: custom 4-layer strided CNN (two-stream, weight-shared) + LSTM actor-critic, trained from scratch with batched A2C (+ supervised pre-training of the conv base)
setting.training_data: On-policy RL in simulators (up to 4·10^7 frames; 16 parallel environments). Supervised pre-training of the conv base on precomputed House3D/SUNCG images with depth and segmentation labels: text says ≈20,000 images, Table I says a dataset size of 2·10^5. DeepMind Lab was also used for pre-training and comparisons.
setting.observation: monocular RGB (84×84 in DeepMind Lab, 174×174 in AI2-THOR/House3D) plus an RGB goal image; depth and segmentation used only as auxiliary training targets
setting.action_space: discrete: forward/backward/strafe-left/strafe-right (e.g. 0.5/-0.2/0.35 m), rotate ±30°, camera tilt ±30°, with Gaussian actuation noise in continuous space; grid variant in AI2-THOR uses ±0.33 m moves and ±90° rotations
setting.simulator: DeepMind Lab, AI2-THOR (grid and authors' continuous modification), House3D (SUNCG)
setting.privileged: none at test time (depth/segmentation only as training targets). Agents are evaluated on the same scenes and targets used in training.

numbers_note: No results tables. All results are training curves in figures (average episode length or return vs. frames, Monte Carlo over 100 rollouts); no SR/SPL. Text-only quantitative statements: (1) AI2-THOR grid, 4 scenes with multiple targets: A2CAT-VN 'found the optimal solution after approximately 5·10^5 frames', whereas Zhu et al. (ICRA 2017) 'was not able to converge even in 7·10^6 steps'; training took ~1 day vs 3 days. (2) House3D/SUNCG room-goal navigation on 16 houses: A2CAT-VN reached an average episode length of 200 in '≈3·10^6 frames', vs '≈8·10^6 frames' without the additional VN auxiliary tasks (A2C+UNREAL). None are standard benchmark metrics, so none were entered.
results: On four AI2-THOR scenes with a grid action space, A2CAT-VN converged to optimal paths in about 5·10^5 frames (~1 day of training). The Zhu et al. 2017 target-driven baseline did not converge within 7·10^6 steps (3 days). On 16 SUNCG houses in House3D with room-type image goals, the navigation-specific auxiliary tasks roughly halved training frames versus A2C+UNREAL (≈3·10^6 vs ≈8·10^6 frames to reach an average episode length of 200). The agent also learned multi-target image-goal navigation in a noisy, continuous AI2-THOR bedroom with randomly placed targets.
limitations: Evaluation is in training environments with training targets only. There is no test on unseen scenes or unseen goals, and no standard SR/SPL metrics; results are shown only as training curves.
No ablation of individual auxiliary tasks, pre-training or curriculum. The auxiliary-task comparison mixes these factors, and the authors defer an ablation to future work.

The comparison to Zhu et al. uses different, larger scenes than the original paper. Continuous AI2-THOR experiments were limited to a single scene because the simulator was too slow. No real-robot validation.
builds_on: Learning to Navigate in Complex Environments (Mirowski et al. 2016)
compares_to: Target-driven visual navigation (Zhu et al., ICRA 2017)
